title: A colleague who smells of alcohol before theatre

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: GMC Good medical practice (in effect Jan 2024; updated Dec 2024)
GMC Raising and acting on concerns (2012; updated Dec 2024)

related.id: MB-177 Angry relative after a delayed diagnosis
related.why: Another conversation where honesty protects patients

related.id: MB-178 Handover of a deteriorating patient

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the elective general surgery list
brief.scenario: Your fellow core trainee, Dr Rhys Hartley, is due to assist on the 8.30 am list and to do a supervised inguinal hernia repair. As he changes, you notice he smells strongly of alcohol, his speech is slightly slurred and he stumbles putting on his clogs. The consultant, Miss Venn, is in the anaesthetic room.
brief.task: Talk to Dr Hartley about your concerns and agree what happens next. The examiner may ask you questions at the end.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Patients first, then your colleague. Private, honest, kind, and firm: he doesn't work today, and the consultant must know.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Agreeing to keep it quiet if he promises to "just assist".
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Rhys, can we have a quick word in here, just us?"

grid.label: Setting and opening
grid.fail: Challenges him in front of others, or opens with "Are you drunk?"
grid.pass: Finds a private space, asks how he is, and gives him the chance to speak.
grid.high: Keeps a calm, non-judgemental tone throughout, with no accusation, so he stays in the conversation.

grid.label: Stating the concern honestly
grid.fail: Hints vaguely, or says nothing and hopes someone else notices.
grid.pass: Names what he has noticed: the smell of alcohol, slurred speech, unsteadiness; says he is worried.
grid.high: Sticks to observed facts, acknowledges he may be embarrassed, and is honest that this can't be ignored.

grid.label: Patient safety first (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Lets him scrub, assist or see patients.
grid.pass: States clearly he can't do any clinical work today, including assisting.
grid.high: Explains that the duty to protect patients overrides loyalty to a colleague.

grid.label: Escalating to the consultant now
grid.fail: Leaves it for him to decide whether to tell anyone.
grid.pass: Informs Miss Venn before the list starts, offering to go with him; she arranges cover.
grid.high: Knows the next steps: clinical or medical director if local action is inadequate, and the GMC in the circumstances set out in para 16.

grid.label: Exploring and empathy
grid.fail: Lectures him, or ignores cues about his life outside work.
grid.pass: Asks what's been going on; acknowledges the cue about his girlfriend; listens.
grid.high: Gently asks how much and how often he's been drinking, without judging.

grid.label: His safety and support
grid.fail: Lets him drive home, or offers no support.
grid.pass: Stops him driving; arranges a taxi or someone to collect him; suggests his GP and occupational health.
grid.high: Suggests confidential support for doctors and his educational supervisor; reminds him he should seek independent advice on fitness for work.

grid.label: Handling pressure to cover for him
grid.fail: Agrees to keep it quiet if he promises to go home.
grid.borderline: Insists he stops working but agrees not to tell the consultant.
grid.pass: Holds the line kindly: he can't keep this between them, and explains why.
grid.high: Acknowledges his fear for his training, and explains that seeking help early is the best protection.

grid.label: Record and follow-up
grid.fail: Makes no record and never checks on him again.
grid.pass: Keeps a factual record of what he saw and the steps taken; checks on him later.
grid.high: Knows that raising a concern honestly, on reasonable belief, is justified even if mistaken, and protected by whistleblowing law.

high.text: I'll be straight with you, because I care about you and our patients. I can smell alcohol, your speech is slurred, and you stumbled. I know that's embarrassing to hear, but I can't ignore it.

failures.consequence: Safety-critical: an impaired doctor at the operating table puts the patient at risk.

failures.move: Promising to keep it between the two of you.
failures.consequence: Puts loyalty above patient safety and leaves him without help.
Safety-critical: risk to him and the public.

failures.move: Confronting him in front of theatre staff.
failures.consequence: Humiliates him and makes denial more likely.

recovery.line: Rhys, I'm going to tell Miss Venn now. I'd rather we did it together.
Sorry, that came out wrong. I'm worried about you, and I need to tell you what I've noticed.

knowledge.fact: Concern that a colleague may not be fit to practise and may be putting patients at risk: seek advice and, if still concerned, report it (para 75).
The duty to protect patients overrides personal and professional loyalties; you don't need proof (para 10).
Risk of serious harm: report immediately, first to the consultant in charge, or the clinical or medical director (paras 12–13).
GMC if the local body is part of the problem, local action is inadequate, or the risk is immediate and serious (para 16).
A disclosure in the public interest that someone's health or safety is endangered can be protected (ERA s43B(1)(d)).

recall.say: "You can't work today, and Miss Venn needs to know. Let's tell her together."
do: No clinical work; consultant told now

numbers.meaning: reasons to go to the GMC: local body involved, inadequate action, immediate risk

recall.finish: Consultant informed, cover arranged, factual record, follow-up call.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format; introduce yourself and confirm identity

sources.name: GMC: Good medical practice 2024 (Domain 3: Colleagues, culture and safety)
sources.supports: Act promptly if patient safety or dignity is, or may be, seriously compromised; if you have concerns that a colleague may not be fit to practise and may be putting patients at risk, ask for advice from a colleague, your defence body or the GMC, and if still concerned, report it in line with workplace policy and the GMC guidance on raising concerns (para 75); take care of your own health, recognising if you may not be fit for work, and seek independent professional advice about fitness for work rather than relying on your own assessment (para 78)

sources.name: GMC: Raising and acting on concerns about patient safety (Part 1: Raising a concern)
sources.supports: Duty to raise concerns where patient safety is compromised by the practice of colleagues (para 7); the duty to put patients' interests first overrides personal and professional loyalties; the law protects those raising genuine concerns; you do not need to wait for proof: a concern raised honestly, on reasonable belief and through appropriate channels is justified even if mistaken (para 10); if patients are or may be at risk of death or serious harm, report to the appropriate person immediately (para 12); raise first with your manager or an appropriate officer, such as the consultant in charge of the team or the clinical or medical director; trainees may use a named person in the training organisation (para 13); be clear, honest and objective (para 14); keep a record of the concern and steps taken (para 15); contact the GMC if the local body is part of the problem, local action is inadequate, or there is an immediate serious risk (para 16); advice from a senior colleague, the GMC helpline, a defence body or a professional association (para 18)

sources.name: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 (c. 23), inserting Part IVA into the Employment Rights Act 1996 (s43B)
sources.supports: A qualifying disclosure is information which, in the reasonable belief of the worker, is made in the public interest and tends to show, among other things, that the health or safety of any individual has been, is being or is likely to be endangered (ERA 1996 s43B(1)(d)); protection from detriment and dismissal

partner.opening: Dr Hartley is getting changed. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Dr Rhys Hartley, 28, a first-year core surgical trainee. You were out until 2 am for a friend's birthday and drank heavily; you drove in this morning. Opening line: "Morning! Ready for the hernia?" Emotional state: cheerful at first, then defensive ("I'm fine"), then frightened. Pressure lines, in order: "I'll just assist, the reg can operate"; "Please don't tell Miss Venn, I'll lose my training number." Hidden facts, only on the right question: your girlfriend Anna left two months ago; you've been drinking most nights since; you failed an exam last month. Give the cue "Things have been rubbish since Anna left" once. If asked how you got here, say you drove and plan to drive home. If the candidate is firm but kind, agree to go with them to tell Miss Venn. If they agree to cover for you, relax and head to theatre.

reveals.trigger: Asks how he is, in private
reveals.finding: "Bit rough. Mate's birthday. I'm fine to work, honestly."
"She left two months ago. I've been having a few most nights. And I failed my exam."

reveals.trigger: Asks how he got to work
reveals.finding: "Drove. I'll be fine to drive back."

reveals.trigger: Offers to tell the consultant together

push.question: What would you do if he refused and walked into theatre?
push.expect: Tell the consultant in charge immediately so he is stopped; if local action is inadequate, the clinical or medical director; the GMC in the circumstances in para 16.

push.question: What if you're wrong and he hadn't been drinking?
push.expect: A concern raised honestly, on reasonable belief and through appropriate channels is justified even if mistaken; the law protects genuine concerns.

curveballs.prompt: "I'll just assist. The reg can do the operation."
curveballs.safeAnswer: No clinical work at all today, including assisting.

curveballs.prompt: Miss Venn says: "Just keep an eye on him."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Respectfully states the risk again; if she doesn't act, raises it with the clinical or medical director.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes tearful and says he drinks every night to sleep.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges it; still no work today; encourages confidential help and his GP; offers to stay with him until the taxi comes.
